The idea is the same as in the [[ge-rectas|plane]]: a point to fix where it is and one or two vectors to say which way it extends.

Durante años, la manera de representar e: For years, the way of representing space on paper was a military secret. Gaspard Monge, a teacher at the engineering school of Mézières, found around 1765 a method for solving on drawn plans the fortification problems officers solved with very long calculations: projecting every object onto two perpendicular planes. The French army classified it, and descriptive geometry was not taught publicly until 1795. Monge himself was among the first to write planes and lines systematically with equations, which is what this topic does: replacing the drawing with the calculation.
Dos planos, una recta y un plano, dos re: Two planes, a line and a plane, two lines: in every case it is a system of equations, and how they are placed is the same as how many solutions it has. The Greek letters $\alpha$ (alpha) and $\beta$ (beta) are any two numbers, not both zero at once.

Why it works: if a point satisfies both equations, it also satisfies any mixture of them. So every plane in this family contains the line, and by giving values to $\alpha$ and $\beta$ you get them all.

It is the shortcut for problems of the kind “the plane containing $r$ and passing through the point $Q$”: you substitute $Q$ and isolate the ratio between $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
Estas cuentas son las que hace, millones: These are the calculations a program drawing in three dimensions makes, millions of times a second. To know what is seen at each pixel a line is fired from the eye and you look for where it meets the planes of the scene: it is exactly the “line and plane” case of this topic, and it is worked out with code in [[gfx-trazado]]. 3D printers do the opposite: they cut the part with horizontal planes, layer by layer.
